newsitem.title: CHINA: China expels corrupt official from Communist Party.
newsitem.headline: China expels corrupt official from Communist Party.

text.p: China's ruling Communist Party has stripped a senior official of his membership for corruption and state media said on Friday that Huang Jicheng would likely face criminal charges.
Huang, 65, a senior official in the hierarchy of the Beijing municipality, was the latest in a stream of officials in the Chinese capital to fall victim to a drive to stamp out graft.
The party's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection had expelled Huang "for serious corruption in violation of the law and party discipline", the People's Daily newspaper said.
He was also sacked as vice chairman of the Beijing Municipal Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, a largely honorary advisory body, it said.

Huang, who had also been chairman of the Beijing Urban Management Committee since 1983, was accused of taking huge bribes while in office and of committing other economic offences that were still under investigation, the newspaper said.
The Supreme People's Procuratorate was investigating the case and state media hinted that Huang, who was ordered to stop work last February, had been detained.
Several other senior Beijing officials have been sacked or arrested for alleged corruption, much of it involving kickbacks from huge construction projects in the capital.

Scandal first surfaced among Beijing's rulers in April, 1995 when Vice Mayor Wang Baosen committed suicide after coming under investigation for corruption and embezzlement involving as much as $37 million.

Beijing Communist Party boss Chen Xitong was forced to resign shortly afterwards and Vice Mayor Zhang Baifa said this week that Chen could be punished for dereliction of duty -- in a further disgrace for an official who was once among China's most influential men.
Zhang said Chen was unlikely to face criminal charges since investigations into the man who presided over China's capital for most of the 1980s had uncovered no evidence of more serious wrongdoing.
Corruption, virtually eliminated in the years after the puritan communists came to power in 1949, has staged a comeback in the past two decades in the wake of economic reforms.
Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin has warned that corruption is a "virus" that theatens the party's grip on power.
China's parliament is set next week to pass an anti- corruption bill, part of a series of measures to tackle graft.
The draft Law on Administrative Supervision would allow prosecutors to investigate a suspect's bank account and ask courts to freeze them when investigating graft, bribery and embezzlement.
State media said this week that China's top prosecutors have vowed to crack down on corruption among the ranks of leading officials in the government and ruling Communist Party.

In the first 11 months of 1996, Chinese prosecutors had begun action in 77,611 cases of corruption, bribery and economic crime and had dealt with 33,879 cases, up 9.4 percent year-on-year, the media said.
